title: Task Fidelity Scaling Laws — Kobie Crawdord, Snorkel
talk_summary: Snorkel argues that task/data quality dominates agentic training and evaluation outcomes, showing accepted (high-quality) tasks produce cleaner, more meaningful failures and a 5x larger RL uplift than rejected tasks. They define quality via four criteria (achievable, non-trivial, functionally correct, reliable environment) and gate tasks through automated acceptance tests, plus rubric-based human+LLM judge agreement.

takeaways.what_they_do: They run every candidate task through tests for four criteria (achievable, non-trivial, functionally correct, reliable environment) and only accepted tasks enter the usable pool; rejected ones are bucketed separately.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If a task passes all of those tests, then we consider it an accepted task
takeaways.numbers: Accepted tasks: ~2x tool calls, lower pass rate, more output tokens; RL uplift 6% vs 1% (5x)

takeaways.technique: Failure-mode taxonomy to separate real defects from degenerate failures
takeaways.what_they_do: They categorize failures (logic error, incomplete task, environment/degenerate) and compare distributions across task quality buckets, so a low pass rate isn't mistaken for model weakness when it's environmental noise.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the accepted tasks are producing cleaner failures

takeaways.technique: Underspecified-task detection as a rejection reason
takeaways.what_they_do: They identify underspecification — tests expecting things never requested, or implicit dependencies not in context — as a top cause of rejected tasks that look 'harder' but are actually broken.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the tests don't match with the the requested task set up

takeaways.what_they_do: They build longer rubrics used by both LLM judges and human annotators, then measure inter-annotator agreement between humans and between LLM judges and humans as a quality metric.

takeaways.technique: Environment reliability as a first-class acceptance criterion
takeaways.what_they_do: They treat environment reliability as one of four quality criteria, containerizing for reproducibility and isolation, and explicitly exclude failures no model could solve.
